summary: Lists requirements for supporting customer RSVP and RSVP-TE signaling over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN. Customers want end-to-end quality of service, such as reserved bandwidth, across a provider network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo asks what it would take for a service provider to offer a customer reserved bandwidth across a VPN. It describes two ways to do it and lists the things any implementation would have to handle.

questions: how do you support qos over vpn
subtitle: What a service provider needs to give a customer reserved bandwidth across a VPN.

tldr.problem: A provider wants to sell a guaranteed bandwidth and a quality of service between a customer's sites across its BGP/MPLS IP-VPN, but the current VPN architecture has no way to run a customer's reservation signalling inside it.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out two models, one where the customer's reservation is carried as native IP and one where the customer gets a labelled path, and in both cases the reservation is aggregated onto transport paths that the provider already runs.
tldr.outcome: It then lists the requirements a solution must meet, covering path selection, admission control, protection, reoptimization and management, and states that a specification is out of scope.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Some service providers want to build a service that guarantees a quality of service and a bandwidth from a local customer edge to a remote customer edge through the network. The customer edge includes the network client equipment owned and operated by the service provider, but it may not be part of the provider's MPLS network. Customers today expect to run triple-play services such as internet access, telephone and television through BGP/MPLS IP-VPNs, and as those services evolve the requirements for an end-to-end quality of service grow with them.

Depending on the application, whether voice, video or a bandwidth-guaranteed data pipe, a native IP flow using RSVP or an end-to-end constrained MPLS traffic engineering path may be needed. An RSVP path can provide quality of service guarantees and reserve enough bandwidth for the data, and an end-to-end MPLS-TE path can also guarantee bandwidth and provide extended functions such as MPLS fast reroute, which maintains service continuity around node and link failures including the link between the customer edge and the provider edge. An RSVP session between two customer edges may also be mapped and tunnelled into an MPLS-TE path across the provider network.

Two advantages follow from this model. Customers can use the service while using private addresses and global addresses, and the traffic is tunnelled through the provider backbone, so customer traffic and route confidentiality are maintained.

The document defines a reference model, example application scenarios and detailed requirements for a solution supporting customer RSVP and RSVP-TE over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN. A specification for a solution is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer asks for a path with a set amount of bandwidth. The provider's own core network already has paths with bandwidth set aside, so the customer's request is mapped onto one of those rather than carried end to end by itself.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of the Model
sections.content: The document uses the BGP/MPLS IP-VPN terminology from RFC 4364 and the Path Computation Element terms from RFC 4655, and defines the following. A traffic engineering label switched path is a path across a traffic engineered network. An MPLS-TE path is such a path in a multiprotocol label switching network. A customer RSVP path is a native RSVP path with a bandwidth reservation of X for customers. A customer traffic engineering path is an end-to-end MPLS-TE path for customers. A provider traffic engineering path is a transport path between two provider edge routers. A label switching router is a router that switches labelled packets, with the head-end being the ingress router and the tail-end the egress router.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of path appear in the text: the path the customer asks for, the path the provider uses across its own network, and the router at each end of it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Two Models
sections.content:
Providers want to deliver triple-play services with quality of service guarantees, and they have two ways in mind: an RSVP signalling for native IP flows, and an RSVP-TE signalling for customer traffic engineered paths, both over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN.

A customer RSVP path with a bandwidth reservation of X can carry voice traffic. To recover in under 50 ms from link, node and shared risk link group failures, and to give strict quality of service guarantees, a customer traffic engineered path with bandwidth X between data centres or customer sites can carry voice and video traffic. Providers or customers can therefore choose whichever model meets their requirements.

The difficulty is scalability. When a provider offers a customer RSVP path between hosts or customer edges over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN, the customer edge or host requests an end-to-end path with a reservation of X to the remote end. If that signalling is to run inside a VPN, the provider network faces scalability issues, because routers have to retain RSVP state per customer. To solve that, several customer reservations can be aggregated at a provider edge, where the head-end of a provider path can perform admission control using the aggregated reservations, following the method described in RFC 4804. A reservation request from inside a VRF instance can then be aggregated onto a provider path that is pre-established, resized on request or triggered by the request. Providers, however, cannot currently provide a customer RSVP path over the VRF instance as defined in RFC 4364, and the current architecture does not support an RSVP instance running in the context of a VRF to process RSVP messages and integrated services.

The customer traffic engineered path has a similar set of problems. A customer path can be aggregated by a provider path at a provider edge, that is, as a hierarchical path, in which case only the provider edge keeps the state of customer RSVP sessions. It cannot be aggregated in some cases, for instance with continuous paths, in which case both the provider routers and the provider edges keep that state. It can also be aggregated by a non-traffic-engineered path such as an LDP path, in which case only the provider edge keeps the state, on the assumption that there is always enough bandwidth in the core.

Providers also cannot currently offer a customer traffic engineered path over the VRF instance as defined in RFC 4364, because the architecture does not support an RSVP-TE instance running in the context of a VRF to process RSVP messages and trigger establishment of the customer path across the core. And if every customer path triggers the establishment or resizing of a provider path, the provider network faces scalability problems from maintaining many provider paths and signalling all of them dynamically.

The difference between the two models is in the data path. In the customer RSVP path model, data packets between customer edges are forwarded as native IP packets, not labelled packets. In the customer traffic engineered path model, they are forwarded as labelled IP packets. Depending on the service level and the requirements, providers should be able to choose traffic engineered or non-traffic-engineered paths in the backbone, based on their policy and on what the nodes support.
sections.plainLanguage: The obstacle is that a reservation per customer would need per-customer state on every router. The fix is to gather many customer reservations into a few provider paths, so that only the provider edge routers keep customer state.

sections.title: Application Scenarios
sections.content:
Six scenarios are worked through, and in all of them it is the provider's responsibility to ensure that enough bandwidth is available for the customer's application.

In the first, a customer runs a voice application between its sites and establishes a customer path as a primary with a second as a backup, so that the loss of the link between the provider edge and the customer edge, or of the provider edge itself, is covered by the backup. Generally, customer RSVP paths are used by customers and provider paths by the provider.

In the second, one provider carries voice and video between its own sites and establishes a customer path with preemption priority 0 and 100 Mbit/s for voice, and another with preemption priority 1 and 200 Mbit/s for video, while the network provider pre-establishes provider paths with preemption priority 0 and 1 Gbit/s for voice and priority 1 and 2 Gbit/s for video. The provider paths should support Diffserv-aware traffic engineering, and the provider edge head-ends choose an appropriate provider path based on the preemption priority, so that the customer voice path is associated with the first provider path and the customer video path with the second. If the customer and the provider have different preemption priorities, the provider's policy wins; where the provider does not support preemption priorities, such priorities should be ignored.

In the third, a provider sets up customer paths with preemption priority 0 and 100 Mbit/s for voice and priority 1 and 200 Mbit/s for video between several of its sites, while the network provider pre-establishes provider paths of 1 and 2 Gbit/s for the same two classes, with the provider paths supporting Diffserv-aware traffic engineering. All provider edges choose an appropriate provider path based on preemption priority, and diversely routed customer paths are established to minimise the disruption from a single network failure, so fast reroute is not necessarily required here. Unconstrained paths with zero bandwidth are also applicable, and load balancing between two hosts can be done by setting up full-mesh customer paths.

In the fourth, a customer has two hosts attached to two customer edges that connect to two provider edges within a VRF instance belonging to the same VPN. The requesting host asks for an RSVP path with a reservation of X, and that request is aggregated onto a pre-established provider path, following procedures similar to RFC 4804. There may be several provider paths with different Diffserv-aware traffic engineering class types, and local policies can map the incoming request to the provider path with the right class type. The request may also be started by the customer edge devices themselves.

The fifth and sixth scenarios cover the case where the customer path runs over a path that is not traffic engineered: an RSVP path over a non-traffic-engineered path, and an RSVP-TE path over a non-traffic-engineered path. In these cases it may be hard to guarantee end-to-end bandwidth, because resources are shared.
sections.plainLanguage: The six worked examples cover the practical cases: a backup path for voice, strict bandwidth and priority guarantees, spreading traffic over several paths, aggregating a reservation onto a transport path, and running over paths that carry no traffic engineering at all.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
For the customer traffic engineered path model the requirements are numerous. A solution must be able to decide which provider paths a provider edge uses for a customer path, choosing based on local policies such as preemption priority, affinity, class type and, in the data plane, the Diffserv code point or traffic class bits. It should support graceful restart, so that customer path traffic keeps flowing while a provider edge restarts, with the mechanisms for this architecture described in RFC 3473, RFC 3623 and RFC 4781. It must be able to reroute a customer path on link, node and shared risk link group failures or on preemption, whether controlled by the customer edge or the provider edge, and in a dual-homed environment it must be able to reroute against a failure of the customer-provider link or of the provider edge when another link or edge is available.

Fast reroute must be supported for a customer path over a VRF instance, because such a path traverses several provider edges and routers even when tunnelled over a provider path, so the customer's head-end needs link protection, provider edge node protection and customer edge node protection.

Admission control must exist at the head-end of a provider path, since customer paths could try to reserve more bandwidth than the provider path has. The head-end should control how many customer paths it admits from a customer edge and how much bandwidth they may reserve, either leaving the natural admission of the provider path or setting a cap, under which it can either reserve the smaller of the cap and the requested bandwidth when it is available, or reject the customer path. In a core network built on LDP, admission control must also exist at the provider edge, with a configurable limit on how much bandwidth customer paths may reserve for a given VRF instance and, optionally, on the total between two provider edges.

Policy control at the provider edge must let it limit the rate of RSVP messages per customer edge, accept and map or reject requests for a given affinity, accept and map or reject requests with specified setup or preemption priorities, accept or reject requests for fast reroute, ignore requested priorities and affinities and choose a provider path by local policy, and map customer traffic class bits onto the transport path's traffic class bits in the data plane. The Path Computation Element architecture should be supported, with customer edges and provider edges or routers acting as clients and the latter possibly as elements, along with dynamic discovery of the elements that know the VPN routes. Diversely routed customer paths over the VRF instance must be possible, over provider paths that are fully disjoint inside the provider network, which allows traffic to be load balanced across them and gives path protection. The optimal path must be supported, computed on the traffic engineering metric for a traffic engineered path and on the IGP metric for an LDP path. Reoptimization must be supported and done with make-before-break, whether timer-based, event-driven or triggered by the customer. Diffserv-aware traffic engineering must be supported, so that traffic from a given Diffserv class on its own customer path can use the resources of that class on both shortest and non-shortest paths and follow paths meeting constraints specific to the class; where the provider and the customer have different bandwidth constraint models, only the provider's model should be supported.

For the customer RSVP path model, admission control must exist at the ingress provider edge, with provider edges controlling RSVP messages per VRF instance. Aggregating customer paths onto provider paths should be supported, with those provider paths established manually or dynamically by operators or triggered by customer messages, and supporting Diffserv-aware traffic engineering. Non-traffic-engineered paths should be supported, and local policies may map the customer's reserved flow to the path with the appropriate traffic class. The solution should not change the RSVP messages between the local and remote customer edge, so that customers see the messages transparently.

Requirements common to both models cover routing on the customer-provider links, where static routing, BGP, OSPF and, for the RSVP-TE case, OSPF-TE are all listed as supported configurations. The solution should avoid adding so much complexity to the operating network that it affects stability, should avoid affecting existing RSVP and MPLS-TE mechanisms so that migration or co-existence is smooth, and should limit its effect on network scalability, noting that a Path Computation Element offers a way to offload path computation and so helps with that.

Scalability must be addressed for RSVP, in terms of the number of messages and retained state, for RSVP-TE, in terms of the number of control messages, retained state and message size, and for BGP, in terms of the number of routes, flaps and overload events. Performance should be evaluated on the degree of path optimality, path setup time, failure and restoration time, and the effect of the added overhead on the control plane and on the forwarding plane. Management must be addressed with a MIB module for the control plane, including the mapping of provider paths and customer paths and bandwidth monitoring, and with diagnostic tools such as traceroute and ping; routers must support the MIB module per VRF instance, providers must be able to collect that information from a customer edge per customer, and control-plane and data-plane failures of customer paths over a VRF instance must be detectable. MPLS operations, administration and maintenance for customer paths must be supported within the VRF context.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is long but the shape is simple: choose the right transport path, refuse what will not fit, protect against failures, keep the paths optimal, and make it all manageable and visible to the operator.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any solution should meet three general security requirements: it should not divulge the provider's topology information to the customer network, it should minimise the provider network's vulnerability to denial of service attacks, and it should minimise the misconfiguration of the Diffserv marking, preemption and holding priorities of customer traffic.

In the control plane, in both models the provider edge receives RSVP control packets from the customer edge. If that customer edge is a router the provider does not trust, the provider edge must be able to limit the rate and number of these control packets. In the data plane, in the customer traffic engineered path model, the provider edge receives labelled data packets from the customer edge, and for an untrusted customer edge it must be able to limit their rate, while for a trusted one it may do so. The provider edge must drop labelled packets whose label was not assigned over the link on which they were received, and must be able to police traffic to the profile associated with the path on which it arrives.

Flooding RSVP and RSVP-TE control packets from malicious customers must be avoided, so a provider edge must isolate the impact of one customer's packets from those of other customers. Where customer paths are diversely routed over VRF instances, the VRF should indicate to the customer edge how that diversity was provided.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer must not be able to flood the provider with reservation messages, nor send labelled packets with a label the provider never gave it. The provider edge rate limits and drops anything that does not match what it assigned.

items.title: Fast recovery
items.text: A customer sets up a backup path so a link or provider edge failure does not stop the voice service.

items.title: Strict quality of service
items.text: Voice and video paths with fixed bandwidth and preemption priority, mapped onto transport paths with the same priority.

items.title: Load balancing
items.text: Several paths with different priorities spread the traffic between the same pair of sites.

items.title: Reservation aggregation
items.text: A customer reservation is gathered onto a transport path, chosen by local policy from the class types available.

items.title: Over a non-engineered path
items.text: An RSVP path carried over a plain path, where end-to-end bandwidth is hard to guarantee because resources are shared.

items.title: Engineered over a non-engineered path
items.text: An RSVP-TE path carried over a plain path, with the same limitation on guaranteed bandwidth.
